name: PneumA

sections.publication:
- Title:Comparison of 8 vs 15 Days of Antibiotic Therapy for Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia in Adults: A Randomized Trial
- Acronym:PneumA
- Year:2003
- Journal published in:JAMA
- Citation:Chastre J, Wolff M, Fagon JY, Chevret S, Thomas F, Wermert D, et al; PneumA Trial Group. Comparison of 8 vs 15 days of antibiotic therapy for ventilator-associated pneumonia in adults: a randomized trial. JAMA. 2003 Nov 19;290(19):2588-98.
sections.context:
Background: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) is a frequent ICU-acquired infection, associated with prolonged ventilation, longer ICU stay, and substantial mortality risk. Historically, VAP was commonly treated with prolonged antibiotic courses (often 14–21 days), driven by concern for relapse—particularly with Gram-negative pathogens. Prolonged broad-spectrum therapy increases antimicrobial selection pressure, fostering multidrug resistance and superinfection, while robust evidence supporting long durations was limited.

Research Question/Hypothesis: Hypothesis: an 8-day antibiotic course is noninferior to a 15-day course for microbiologically confirmed VAP, for both 28-day mortality and microbiologically documented recurrent pulmonary infection. Stewardship hypothesis: shorter therapy reduces antibiotic exposure and may reduce emergence of resistant pathogens without compromising patient-important outcomes.

Why This Matters: Defines an evidence-based “default” duration for VAP therapy—an area historically dominated by convention. Directly links treatment duration to antibiotic-sparing outcomes (antibiotic-free days) and microbiological consequences (multiresistant pathogens), relevant to ICU-level antimicrobial stewardship. Addresses pathogen-specific concern (nonfermenting Gram-negative bacilli) that could plausibly require longer therapy, informing nuanced duration decisions rather than a single rule for all VAP.

sections.methods:
- Research Question:In adults with microbiologically confirmed VAP receiving appropriate initial empirical antibiotics, is an 8-day antibiotic course noninferior to a 15-day course for 28-day all-cause mortality and microbiologically documented recurrent pulmonary infection?
- Study Type:Multicentre, randomised, controlled, noninferiority trial; double-blind to group allocation until day 8; conducted in 51 ICUs in France.
- Population:Setting:Adult ICUs (France); mechanically ventilated patients evaluated for suspected VAP; diagnosis confirmed by quantitative culture from bronchoscopic sampling.Inclusion criteria:Age ≥18 years; ≥48 hours of mechanical ventilation; new and persistent infiltrate on chest radiography plus ≥1 of: purulent tracheal secretions, temperature ≥38.3°C, leukocyte count >10,000/µL (in ARDS with difficult radiological interpretation, ≥1 of these criteria sufficed); positive quantitative cultures from bronchoalveolar lavage (≥104CFU/mL) or protected specimen brush/catheter (≥103CFU/mL); initiation within 24 hours of bronchoscopy of appropriate empirical antibiotics active against the causative organism(s).Key exclusions:Pregnancy; concurrent enrolment in another trial; little chance of survival (SAPS II >65); neutropenia (leukocyte count <1000/µL or neutrophils <500/µL); AIDS stage 3 (CDC 1993); immunosuppressants or long-term corticosteroids (≥0.5 mg/kg/day for >1 month); extrapulmonary infection diagnosed between days 1–3 requiring prolonged (>8 days) antimicrobial therapy; attending physician declined full life support; early-onset pneumonia (within first 5 days of mechanical ventilation) with no antimicrobial therapy in the preceding 15 days.Randomisation timing:Randomised 3 days after bronchoscopy (after microbiological confirmation and confirmation of appropriate initial therapy).
  - Setting:Adult ICUs (France); mechanically ventilated patients evaluated for suspected VAP; diagnosis confirmed by quantitative culture from bronchoscopic sampling.
  - Inclusion criteria:Age ≥18 years; ≥48 hours of mechanical ventilation; new and persistent infiltrate on chest radiography plus ≥1 of: purulent tracheal secretions, temperature ≥38.3°C, leukocyte count >10,000/µL (in ARDS with difficult radiological interpretation, ≥1 of these criteria sufficed); positive quantitative cultures from bronchoalveolar lavage (≥104CFU/mL) or protected specimen brush/catheter (≥103CFU/mL); initiation within 24 hours of bronchoscopy of appropriate empirical antibiotics active against the causative organism(s).
  - Key exclusions:Pregnancy; concurrent enrolment in another trial; little chance of survival (SAPS II >65); neutropenia (leukocyte count <1000/µL or neutrophils <500/µL); AIDS stage 3 (CDC 1993); immunosuppressants or long-term corticosteroids (≥0.5 mg/kg/day for >1 month); extrapulmonary infection diagnosed between days 1–3 requiring prolonged (>8 days) antimicrobial therapy; attending physician declined full life support; early-onset pneumonia (within first 5 days of mechanical ventilation) with no antimicrobial therapy in the preceding 15 days.
  - Randomisation timing:Randomised 3 days after bronchoscopy (after microbiological confirmation and confirmation of appropriate initial therapy).
- Intervention:8-day regimen:Antibiotic therapy stopped at the end of day 8 (unless antibiotics were needed for documented pulmonary recurrence before day 8, or for an infection predating VAP where treatment was deemed insufficient).Antibiotic approach:Initial regimen encouraged to include a broad-spectrum β-lactam plus an aminoglycoside or fluoroquinolone when appropriate; de-escalation to narrower therapy based on culture results was encouraged within 48–72 hours.

  - Antibiotic approach:Initial regimen encouraged to include a broad-spectrum β-lactam plus an aminoglycoside or fluoroquinolone when appropriate; de-escalation to narrower therapy based on culture results was encouraged within 48–72 hours.
- Comparison:15-day regimen:Antibiotic therapy continued to the end of day 15 (with the same general approach to initial choice and de-escalation; antibiotics could be extended/changed for documented recurrence or other infections as clinically required).
  - 15-day regimen:Antibiotic therapy continued to the end of day 15 (with the same general approach to initial choice and de-escalation; antibiotics could be extended/changed for documented recurrence or other infections as clinically required).
- Blinding:Allocation was concealed via a central interactive voice response system; group assignment was not communicated to clinicians/investigators until day 8 (at which point continuation vs cessation necessarily revealed group). Implication: potential performance and detection bias after day 8, particularly for clinician-triggered investigations for recurrence.
- Statistics:Noninferiority margin 10% absolute difference for both primary endpoints (28-day mortality and recurrent pulmonary infection); target sample size 400 (200/group) to provide 90% power with alpha risk 10% to exclude a 10% difference, assuming 15-day regimen rates of 40% mortality and 25% recurrent pulmonary infection; 4 planned interim analyses with a repeated one-sided confidence-interval stopping approach; primary analysis by intention-to-treat.
- Follow-Up Period:Daily assessments to day 28 after bronchoscopy; vital status also recorded at hospital discharge and at day 60 after bronchoscopy.
sections.results:
This trial was not stopped early.Recruitment reached the planned sample size (401 analysed) with four pre-specified interim analyses.
Outcome | 8-day regimen | 15-day regimen | Effect | p value / 95% CI | Notes
All-cause mortality, day 28 (primary) | 37/197 (18.8%) | 35/204 (17.2%) | Risk difference 1.6% | 90% CI -3.7 to 6.9 | Noninferiority margin: 10% absolute difference
Pulmonary infection recurrence, day 28 (primary; microbiologically documented) | 57/197 (28.9%) | 53/204 (26.0%) | Risk difference 2.9% | 90% CI -3.2 to 9.1 | Recurrence included relapse and/or superinfection; diagnosis required bronchoscopic sampling with quantitative culture
Pulmonary infection recurrence in nonfermenting Gram-negative bacilli stratum (day 28) | 26/64 (40.6%) | 16/63 (25.4%) | Risk difference 15.2% | 90% CI 3.9 to 26.6 | Signal of higher recurrence with 8 days in this pathogen stratum
Antibiotic-free days to day 28 (mean, SD) | 13.1 (7.4) | 8.7 (5.2) | Mean difference 4.4 days | 95% CI 3.1 to 5.6; P<0.001 | Defined as days alive without antibiotics during the 28-day follow-up
Antibiotic-treatment days to day 28 (mean, SD) | 12.6 (6.2) | 17.1 (4.9) | Mean difference -4.5 days | 90% CI -5.4 to -3.6 | Between-group separation was greatest during days 9–15: 1.3 (2.3) vs 6.6 (1.4); mean difference -5.3 (90% CI -5.6 to -5.0)
Unfavourable outcome by day 28 (death, pulmonary recurrence, or new antibiotics >48 h) | 91/197 (46.2%) | 89/204 (43.6%) | Risk difference 2.6% | 90% CI -5.6 to 10.7 | Composite endpoint; may be influenced by clinician decisions to start antibiotics for non-pulmonary infections
All-cause mortality, day 60 | 50/197 (25.4%) | 57/204 (27.9%) | Risk difference -2.6% | 90% CI -9.8 to 4.7 | No mortality signal beyond day 28
Bronchoscopies performed for suspected recurrence | 120/197 (60.9%) | 93/204 (45.6%) | Not reported | P=0.003 | Differential investigation intensity is relevant for interpreting microbiologically documented recurrence
Multiresistant pathogens among recurrent pulmonary infections | 42.1% | 62.3% | Not reported | P=0.04 | Reported as proportion of recurrent infections involving multiresistant pathogens
- Across all patients, 8 days met the trial’s noninferiority criteria for both 28-day mortality (18.8% vs 17.2%) and microbiologically documented recurrent pulmonary infection (28.9% vs 26.0%).
- Short-course therapy materially reduced antibiotic exposure: antibiotic-free days increased by 4.4 days (95% CI 3.1 to 5.6; P<0.001).
- A clinically important signal emerged in the nonfermenting Gram-negative bacilli stratum, with higher recurrence after 8 days (40.6% vs 25.4%).
sections.internal:
- Randomisation and Allocation:Central interactive voice response system; stratified by centre with block size 4; allocation concealed and not disclosed to investigators/clinicians until day 8.
- Drop out or exclusions (post-randomisation):402 randomised; 1 patient in the 15-day group withdrew consent and was excluded from analysis; analysed population 197 (8-day) vs 204 (15-day).
- Selection effects before randomisation:Randomised 3 days after bronchoscopy and only after confirming both microbiological diagnosis and appropriate initial therapy; 70 patients died before day 3 and 79 had inappropriate initial therapy and were not randomised, enriching for patients who survived and received early adequate antibiotics.
- Performance/Detection Bias:Trial became unblinded at day 8 (continuation vs cessation); bronchoscopy for suspected recurrence was more frequent in the 8-day group (60.9% vs 45.6%; P=0.003), raising the possibility of differential ascertainment of “microbiologically documented” recurrence.
- Protocol Adherence and separation of the variable of interest:Meaningful separation achieved in antibiotic exposure: antibiotic-treatment days to day 28 were 12.6 (6.2) vs 17.1 (4.9) with mean difference -4.5 days (90% CI -5.4 to -3.6); antibiotic-free days were 13.1 (7.4) vs 8.7 (5.2) with mean difference 4.4 days (95% CI 3.1 to 5.6).
- Crossover and additional antibiotics:Despite the “8 vs 15 days” design, substantial subsequent antibiotic use occurred in both groups after the assigned regimen (antibiotic courses introduced after the end of the assigned regimen: 46.3% vs 44.3% among those surviving to end of assigned treatment), reflecting recurrent pulmonary infection and extrapulmonary infections.
- Baseline Characteristics:Illness severity measures at admission were well matched (median SAPS II 47 vs 47; median SOFA 8 vs 8; proportion with septic shock at admission 24.4% vs 21.1%); there was a modest imbalance in sex (men 76.6% vs 67.6%; P=0.046).
- Heterogeneity:Antibiotic choice and pathogen mix were heterogeneous by design; stratified analyses were reported for key microbiological strata (nonfermenting Gram-negative bacilli, MRSA, other bacteria).
- Timing:Randomisation on day 3 prioritised microbiological certainty and ensured “appropriate therapy” at baseline, but means the trial does not address early empiric duration decisions at the moment of clinical VAP suspicion.
- Dose (antimicrobial regimen intensity):Regimen selection was clinician-directed with guidance towards initial broad coverage and de-escalation; this enhances pragmatic relevance but reduces standardisation of antimicrobial “dose” beyond duration.
- Outcome Assessment:Mortality is objective; recurrent pulmonary infection required bronchoscopic sampling with quantitative culture (objective microbiology) but depended on clinician decision to re-bronchoscope (potentially subjective).
- Statistical Rigor:Noninferiority framework with prespecified 10% margin and sequential interim monitoring; sample size target met (401 analysed), but interpretation depends on acceptance of a 10% noninferiority margin for mortality/recurrence.
Conclusion on Internal Validity:Overall, internal validity appearsmoderate: randomisation and allocation concealment were robust and treatment separation was clear, but delayed randomisation (day 3), unblinding after day 8, and differential bronchoscopy frequency create plausible selection and ascertainment biases—most relevant to recurrence outcomes.
sections.external:
- Population Representativeness:Adults in French ICUs with bronchoscopically confirmed VAP and early “appropriate” antibiotics; excludes immunocompromised patients, those with very high predicted mortality (SAPS II >65), and early-onset VAP without prior antibiotics.
- Diagnostic strategy dependence:Requires bronchoscopy with quantitative cultures to define both index VAP and recurrences; applicability is strongest in centres using (or approximating) this diagnostic intensity.
- Applicability across pathogens:Findings support shorter durations for many microbiological strata, but the nonfermenting Gram-negative bacilli subgroup showed higher recurrence with 8 days, suggesting the need for pathogen- and response-informed duration decisions.
- Health-system translation:The pragmatic clinician-selected antibiotic regimens support transferability, but antimicrobial resistance ecology and bronchoscopy availability vary substantially across systems.
Conclusion on External Validity:Generalisability ismoderate: the results are most applicable to adult ICU patients with microbiologically confirmed VAP who receive early adequate antibiotics and can undergo close microbiological reassessment; applicability is more limited in immunosuppressed patients, in settings where VAP is diagnosed clinically without bronchoscopy, and where early inadequate empiric therapy is common.
sections.strengths:
- Strengths:Multicentre design (51 ICUs) with a relatively large analysed sample (n=401) for a VAP duration trial.Microbiological confirmation of VAP and recurrence using quantitative cultures, reducing diagnostic misclassification compared with purely clinical definitions.Clear antibiotic-exposure separation with clinically meaningful stewardship endpoints (antibiotic-free days and total antibiotic days).Pathogen-stratified reporting (nonfermenting Gram-negative bacilli, MRSA, other), aligning with biological plausibility for differential relapse risk.

  - Pathogen-stratified reporting (nonfermenting Gram-negative bacilli, MRSA, other), aligning with biological plausibility for differential relapse risk.

sections.interpretation:
Key points: Stewardship without excess overall mortality: In this selected, microbiologically confirmed VAP cohort, 8 days did not increase 28-day mortality compared with 15 days (18.8% vs 17.2%), while reducing antibiotic exposure (antibiotic-free days 13.1 vs 8.7). Recurrence is pathogen-sensitive: Overall recurrence was similar (28.9% vs 26.0%), but recurrence was higher with 8 days in nonfermenting Gram-negative bacilli (40.6% vs 25.4%), supporting longer or more individualised courses in this stratum. Investigation intensity matters: Higher bronchoscopy frequency in the 8-day group (60.9% vs 45.6%) underscores that recurrence rates in a bronchoscopy-dependent definition can be influenced by clinician behaviour after stopping antibiotics.

sections.controversies:
- Delayed randomisation and “appropriate therapy” enrichment:By randomising at day 3 and excluding patients with inappropriate initial antibiotics or early death, the trial estimates the effect of stopping vs continuing antibiotics among survivors already receiving effective therapy; it does not directly answer how long to treat when initial adequacy is uncertain or delayed.
- Noninferiority design choices:The 10% absolute noninferiority margin for both mortality and recurrent infection creates a trade-off between feasibility and clinical acceptability; the observed differences were small overall, but interpretation depends on whether a 10% margin is considered clinically tolerable.
- Recurrence ascertainment and unblinding:Recurrence required bronchoscopy; after day 8, clinicians knew whether antibiotics were stopped, and bronchoscopy was more frequent in the 8-day group (60.9% vs 45.6%), potentially increasing detection of microbiologically documented recurrence in the short-course arm.
- Pathogen-stratified signal (nonfermenters):The higher recurrence with 8 days in nonfermenting Gram-negative bacilli (40.6% vs 25.4%) is biologically plausible (difficult-to-eradicate organisms) and was aligned with prespecified microbiological strata, yet remains a subgroup finding and must be weighed against the absence of an overall mortality penalty.
- Guideline uptake:Subsequent major international guidelines converged on shorter default durations (typically ~7 days) for VAP while emphasising individualisation for difficult pathogens, slow clinical response, and complications such as abscess/empyema12.
sections.summary:
- Multicentre French ICU noninferiority trial (PneumA) comparing 8 vs 15 days of antibiotics for microbiologically confirmed VAP (401 analysed: 197 vs 204).
- Primary endpoints: 28-day mortality (18.8% vs 17.2%; risk difference 1.6%; 90% CI -3.7 to 6.9) and recurrent pulmonary infection (28.9% vs 26.0%; risk difference 2.9%; 90% CI -3.2 to 9.1).
- Antibiotic exposure was substantially reduced with 8 days: antibiotic-free days 13.1 (7.4) vs 8.7 (5.2), mean difference 4.4 (95% CI 3.1 to 5.6; P<0.001).
- Nonfermenting Gram-negative bacilli subgroup had higher recurrence with 8 days (40.6% vs 25.4%; risk difference 15.2%; 90% CI 3.9 to 26.6).
- Interpretation of recurrence is complicated by differential bronchoscopy for suspected recurrence (60.9% vs 45.6%; P=0.003) after unblinding at day 8.
sections.takeaway:
Chastre et al. provided one of the earliest large, microbiology-anchored demonstrations that short-course therapy for VAP can preserve mortality outcomes while reducing antibiotic exposure. Its landmark influence lies in shifting VAP duration from convention towards evidence-based stewardship, while also highlighting that “shorter is not always safer” for certain microbiological strata (notably nonfermenting Gram-negative bacilli) and that ascertainment of recurrence can be shaped by post-randomisation clinician behaviour.

Overall Summary
  - In microbiologically confirmed VAP treated with early appropriate antibiotics, 8 days was noninferior to 15 days for 28-day mortality and overall recurrence, with more antibiotic-free days; recurrence was higher in nonfermenting Gram-negative bacilli.
